title: About
text:
I am a researcher at Cerema (Centre d’Études et d’Expertise sur les Risques, l’Environnement, la Mobilité et l’Aménagement), affiliated with the UMR MCD (Unité Mixte de Recherche Matériaux et Durabilité des Constructions, Université Gustave Eiffel).
My work lies at the intersection of theoretical mechanics, materials science and scientific computing. It combines the analytical development of micromechanical models with their implementation in open-source libraries, and their application to civil engineering materials — concrete and cement pastes, bituminous mixes, rocks and fractured media.

title: About
text:
Research interests

Micromechanics and homogenization — analytical and semi-analytical methods for predicting effective properties of heterogeneous materials (composites, geomaterials, cracked media)
Eshelby-based models — dilute, Mori–Tanaka, self-consistent and generalized self-consistent schemes for ellipsoidal and crack-like inclusions
Nonlinear and viscoelastic behavior — extension of homogenization methods to nonlinear elasticity and linear viscoelasticity
Scientific software development — open-source libraries in Julia and C++ for computational micromechanics (see Software)

 Browse the software

title: echoes
text:
echoes (Extended Calculator of HOmogEnization Schemes) estimates the effective properties of a random heterogeneous medium from the properties, shapes and volume fractions of its phases. It solves the Eshelby problem at second order (conductivity) and fourth order (elasticity), for isotropic or anisotropic reference media, and feeds the result to a wide family of mean-field schemes. Beyond the effective moduli themselves, it returns their derivatives with respect to the lower-scale moduli — the ingredient a secant-based nonlinear homogenization needs. The numerical core is C++; the modeling is written in Python.

Key features

A wide family of schemes — bounds, dilute and its dual, Mori–Tanaka, self-consistent and asymmetric self-consistent, Maxwell, Ponte Castañeda–Willis, differential
Eshelby at both orders — second order for conductivity, fourth order for elasticity; isotropic and anisotropic media; ellipsoids, cracks, n-layer spheres, generic inclusions
Time and frequency — aging linear viscoelasticity and complex moduli, so a creep or a dynamic modulus follows from the same microstructure
Derivatives of the moduli — the sensitivity of the macroscopic stiffness to the lower-scale moduli, which is what makes secant-based nonlinear homogenization possible
C++ core, Python interface — the numerics are compiled; the modeling is scripted next to NumPy and Matplotlib, in a notebook or a plain script



Installation
Binary wheels for Windows and Linux, Python 3.7 to 3.12, are attached to the Zenodo record the DOI below resolves to — pick the file matching your interpreter, then pip install it.


Documentation
The documentation is a course — tensor calculus, Eshelby and Hill tensors, concentration, schemes, viscoelasticity, nonlinear homogenization — with every tutorial runnable, at jfbarthelemy.github.io/echoes.


License
The wheels are distributed under the ECHOES Academic and Research License: free use for non-commercial research, academic and teaching purposes; any commercial use requires a separate written agreement with the copyright holder. The manual is licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

title: MeanFieldHomogenization.jl
text:
MeanFieldHomogenization.jl predicts the effective elastic, transport and viscoelastic properties of a heterogeneous material from the properties, shapes, orientations and volume fractions of the phases of its microstructure. All the ingredients — inclusion morphologies, localization tensors and homogenization schemes — live under a common abstraction hierarchy with a shared numerical core and a central dispatch mechanism. A microstructure can also serve as the constitutive law at each Gauss point of a finite-element computation. Part of the MicroPoroChemoMechanics ecosystem, built on TensND.jl.

Key features

Hill polarization tensors — ellipsoidal inclusions and infinite cylinders, 2D and 3D, isotropic, anisotropic or transversely isotropic coaxial matrices
Cracks — crack-opening-displacement tensor, compliance contribution, stress and displacement intensity factors for elliptic and ribbon cracks
Transport — second-order Hill tensor with a closed form for any matrix anisotropy
Layered inclusions — n-layer composite spheres and confocal spheroids with imperfect interfaces (perfect, spring, membrane, Kapitza, surface-conductive)
Homogenization schemes — bounds, dilute, Mori–Tanaka, Maxwell, Ponte Castañeda–Willis, self-consistent and asymmetric self-consistent, differential; the cluster model and the equivalent inclusion method for interacting particles
Aging linear Volterra behavior — aging viscoelasticity and hereditary conduction as time-domain Volterra operators with structured ISO/TI/orthotropic kernel storage, in every scheme; and, for non-aging behavior, the Laplace–Carson route with autodiff-capable numerical inversion
Open inclusion contract — any morphology joins every scheme through one of three entry gates (Hill tensor, localization tensors, contribution tensors), whatever computed the answer; the two below are its current tenants, not its limits
Finite-element inclusions — Eshelby problem solved numerically (3-D elliptical crack, sphere with an off-center core) behind a two-backend contract
Neural-surrogate inclusions — a trained multilayer perceptron standing in for the Eshelby response, differentiable with respect to the morphology itself and orders of magnitude cheaper than the finite-element solve it replaces
Prototyping-oriented — ForwardDiff sensitivities with respect to fractions, moduli and inclusion geometry, plus symbolic simplification via SymPy and Symbolics



Try it in the browser
The simplest case the package handles: an isotropic matrix holding isotropic spherical inclusions. The chart gives the effective Young’s modulus as the inclusions take up more of the volume — the Hashin–Shtrikman bounds, which no isotropic mixture of these two phases can leave, and the Mori–Tanaka and self-consistent estimates between them. For spheres all four are closed forms, so the chart computes them in your browser rather than calling the package.

The interactive chart needs JavaScript.



Installation
MeanFieldHomogenization.jl is registered in Julia’s General registry:
using Pkg
Pkg.add("MeanFieldHomogenization")
Optional package extensions activate on weak dependencies: DECUHR.jl with Integrals.jl (adaptive cubature backend), NonlinearSolve.jl (SciML fixed-point algorithms for the self-consistent schemes), SymPy.jl and Symbolics.jl (symbolic computation), MittagLeffler.jl (closed-form time values of the fractional rheological models), two finite-element backends — Ferrite.jl + Gmsh.jl or Gridap.jl + GridapGmsh.jl — and Lux.jl with Optimisers.jl and Zygote.jl to train your own surrogates. Loading a shipped surrogate needs none of them: the trained network carries no machine-learning dependency.


Documentation
Full documentation is available at MicroPoroChemoMechanics.github.io/MeanFieldHomogenization.jl, including a gallery of complete micromechanical models in the Applications section — hydrating cement paste, chloride diffusivity, the interfacial transition zone in concrete, quasi-brittle strength, the elastic limit of concrete, the friction of a granular medium, the strength of a sandstone, bituminous mixtures and aging creep.

title: OptimaSolver.jl
text:
OptimaSolver.jl minimizes a Gibbs energy under linear mass-balance constraints, the problem every chemical equilibrium reduces to. It provides a log-barrier interior-point method, an independent Julia port of the Optima C++ library of Allan Leal (ETH Zürich), and a Newton method on the optimality conditions in the space of the Lagrange multipliers, which ChemistryLab.jl calls by default. Whichever method produced it, an answer is checked by a KKT certificate, and ForwardDiff derivatives pass through the solve to any order. Part of the MicroPoroChemoMechanics ecosystem.

Key features

A certificate, not a stopping test — kkt_certificate checks the optimality conditions at any point, whatever produced it; for a convex problem they are sufficient, so it proves the global minimum
Two methods, one problem — the interior point takes its Newton step through a Schur complement of the diagonal Hessian; the multiplier-space Newton holds bounded species in an active set
A start from a linear program — lp_start solves the pure-phase program by a verified simplex; an impossible budget comes back with its Farkas proof rather than as a failed iteration
Every row at its own scale — each mass balance is judged against what it holds, so a trace nine orders of magnitude below the major elements is kept to its own amount
Exact derivatives — dual numbers in the budget, the data or the parameters return the derivatives of the solution by the implicit-function theorem, nested to any order
Solvents and their solutes — a phase given invert recovers its solutes in one call, through one equation in the ionic strength for activity models of the Debye–Hückel family



Installation
OptimaSolver.jl is registered in Julia’s General registry:
using Pkg
Pkg.add("OptimaSolver")


Credits and license
The interior-point method is an independent port of Optima (github.com/reaktoro/optima, © 2020–2024 Allan Leal), not affiliated with its authors; the Julia port is © 2026 Jean-François Barthélémy, under LGPL-2.1-or-later. Its design — Schur-complement Newton step, filter line search, variable stability classification, implicit-differentiation sensitivity — comes from that library and from Leal, Blunt & LaForce (2014), Efficient chemical equilibrium calculations for geochemical speciation and reactive transport modelling, Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta 131, 301–322, doi:10.1016/j.gca.2014.01.038.

title: DECUHR.jl
text:
DECUHR.jl is a pure-Julia port of the DECUHR algorithm of Espelid & Genz for the automatic adaptive integration of functions with vertex singularities over hyper-rectangular regions — the situation met whenever a Green function is integrated over an inclusion. Where a plain adaptive rule keeps subdividing without ever converging, the algorithm couples the subdivision to an extrapolation that removes the singular contribution. Part of the MicroPoroChemoMechanics ecosystem.

Key features

Vertex singularities — subdivision coupled to an extrapolation in the cell size, which is what removes the singular contribution instead of chasing it; logarithmic singularities too
Hyper-rectangular regions — boxes of dimension 2 to 15, with rules of degree 13 and 11 dedicated to 2D and 3D
Strength known or not — the algebraic exponent can be supplied when the analysis gives it, or estimated from the samples when it does not
Vector-valued integrands — a whole tensor of integrals shares one subdivision history rather than being recomputed component by component
A SciML algorithm — DecuhrAlgorithm plugs into Integrals.jl like any other solver, and ForwardDiff passes through it, estimated exponent included



Installation
DECUHR.jl is registered in Julia’s General registry:
using Pkg
Pkg.add("DECUHR")


Credits and license
The algorithm and the original Fortran 77 routines are due to T. O. Espelid and A. Genz, DECUHR: an algorithm for automatic integration of singular functions over a hyperrectangular region, Numerical Algorithms 8 (1994) 201–220, doi:10.1007/BF02142691. This package is an independent Julia port of that work, under the MIT license, shipping the upstream copyright notice unmodified.

title: TensND.jl
text:
TensND.jl performs tensor calculations of any order and dimension in arbitrary coordinate systems (cartesian, polar, cylindrical, spherical, spheroidal or user-defined). It supports both symbolic computation (SymPy.jl, Symbolics.jl) and numerical evaluation with automatic differentiation (ForwardDiff.jl). The implementation is inspired by the Maple library Tens3d by Jean Garrigues. Part of the MicroPoroChemoMechanics ecosystem.

Key features

Basis types — canonical, rotated, orthogonal, and fully general (non-orthogonal, symbolic)
Tensor algebra — products (⊗, ⊗ˢ, ⊠, ⊠ˢ, ⋅, ⊡, ⊙), change of basis, variance management
Structured tensors — isotropic (TensISO), transversely isotropic (TensTI), orthotropic (TensOrtho) and cubic (TensCubic), storing 2 to 9 coefficients instead of 81 and staying in their class through products and inversion
Symmetry projection — closest isotropic, transversely isotropic, orthotropic or cubic tensor, with the material frame given or recovered by rotation optimization (NLopt.jl)
Differential operators — gradient, symmetric gradient, divergence, Laplacian and Hessian in curvilinear coordinates, symbolically or numerically
Generic type system — the same code path runs on Float64, on symbolic scalars (Sym, Num) and on ForwardDiff.Dual, so sensitivities come for free



Installation
TensND.jl is registered in Julia’s General registry:
using Pkg
Pkg.add("TensND")

title: MicroPoroChemoMechanics
text: MicroPoroChemoMechanics is a GitHub organization of which I am one of the owners. It hosts a collection of Julia packages for multiscale modeling of porous reactive materials — from molecular-level thermodynamic equilibrium to macroscopic poromechanical response. The packages are designed to compose cleanly: they share conventions, are ForwardDiff-compatible, and plug into the SciML ecosystem.

title: MicroPoroChemoMechanics
text:
Core packages

TensND.jl

Symbolic and numerical tensor calculations of any order and dimension in arbitrary coordinate systems, with structured isotropic, transversely isotropic, orthotropic and cubic types, projection onto each symmetry class, and curvilinear differential operators. It is the tensor foundation of the whole ecosystem.


ChemistryLab.jl

Computational chemistry, from formulas to a certified equilibrium — species, reactions and stoichiometric matrices, ThermoFun and Cemdata data downloaded on demand, activity models up to SIT and Pitzer, solid solutions, surface complexation, kinetics and calorimetry, and Gibbs energy minimization returned with a certificate stating what it proves. Every quantity carries its unit, via DynamicQuantities.


MeanFieldHomogenization.jl

Mean-field homogenization framework for heterogeneous materials: Hill polarization tensors for ellipsoidal inclusions and infinite cylinders, crack-opening-displacement tensors with stress and displacement intensity factors, second-order Hill tensors for transport problems, layered spheres and confocal spheroids with imperfect interfaces, aging viscoelasticity and hereditary conduction as Volterra operators, all the classical schemes, and morphologies with no closed form entered by finite elements or a neural surrogate.

title: MicroPoroChemoMechanics
text:
Backend packages

OptimaSolver.jl

Certified Gibbs energy minimization — a log-barrier interior-point method, an independent port of Allan Leal’s Optima C++ library, and a Newton method in the space of the Lagrange multipliers, every answer checked by a KKT certificate, with exact derivatives through the solve. The default equilibrium backend of ChemistryLab.jl.
 


DECUHR.jl

Pure-Julia port of the DECUHR algorithm of Espelid & Genz (Numerical Algorithms 8, 1994, 201–220) for automatic adaptive integration of functions with vertex singularities over hyper-rectangles of dimension 2 to 15. Exposed as a pluggable algorithm for the SciML Integrals.jl ecosystem, and differentiable with ForwardDiff.

The dedicated MPCM-Registry is deprecated and kept only as a frozen historical snapshot; if you added it in the past, remove it with Pkg.Registry.rm("MPCM-Registry").

title: ChemistryLab.jl
text:
ChemistryLab.jl carries a chemical problem from its written formulas to its equilibrium state. Formulas, species, reactions and stoichiometric matrices are first-class objects, thermodynamic data are read from ThermoFun and Cemdata, and equilibrium is computed by Gibbs energy minimization and returned with a certificate stating what it proves. Every quantity carries its unit, and exact ForwardDiff derivatives pass through equilibria, kinetic runs and recipes. Initially focused on cement chemistry — CEM I to CEM V entered from an oxide analysis — its scope is that of aqueous and mineral systems at large. Developed with Anthony Soive and released under LGPL v2.1+. Part of the MicroPoroChemoMechanics ecosystem.

Key features

Formulas, species and reactions — chemical formulas with charge, Unicode and PHREEQC notations; Species and CemSpecies for solution and solid phases; stoichiometric matrices built automatically
Databases on demand — ThermoFun databases downloaded from their publisher on first use and checked against a SHA-256; install_database takes a PHREEQC file
Certified equilibrium — the certificate says what it proves: global minimum, KKT point or self-consistent speciation, each element balance judged against its own total
Activity models — B-dot, Davies, Truesdell–Jones, SIT and Pitzer; SIT and Pitzer solutes solved by Newton, halite solubility within 0.3 % of its measurement
Solid solutions — ideal, Redlich–Kister, regular, sublattice (C–N–A–S–H) and compound-energy (CASH+) models, miscibility gaps detected and located
Surfaces and interfaces — surface complexation, constant-capacitance and diffuse-layer electrostatics, cation exchange and a Donnan layer, checked against PHREEQC
Recipes, kinetics, heat — binders blended, hydrated, carbonated or leached as recipes; Parrott–Killoh and Waller rate laws; isothermal and semi-adiabatic calorimetry



Installation
ChemistryLab.jl is registered in Julia’s General registry. Solving an equilibrium needs an optimization backend, loaded through a package extension; OptimaSolver.jl is the default one, and the one the certificate needs:
using Pkg
Pkg.add(["ChemistryLab", "OptimaSolver"])
using ChemistryLab, OptimaSolver         # OptimaSolver: the default equilibrium backend
Optimization with OptimizationIpopt remains available as a backend. A database is downloaded once, on first use; fetch_databases() prepares a machine for offline work.
